strengths: Clear motivation and elegant architectural design: The key insight to exclude x_j from g_u_j is clever and well-motivated, preserving interpretability of β_j while enabling nonlinear corrections
Novel optimization framework: Parameter elimination approach efficiently reduces bi-level optimization to NN-only optimization, with principled extension to GLMs via IRLS
Solid theoretical framework: Elegantly unifies global summaries (MEM) with local explanations (per-instance), with mathematically sound derivations

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple synthetic datasets with controlled ground truth, three real datasets with error bars and multiple runs, reasonable baselines including recent methods (IMN, LassoNet)
Good ablation study: Demonstrates importance of feature masking and positional encoding on both interpretability and sparsity
Practical implementation considerations: Positional encoding solution addresses computational efficiency, group L2 regularization enables feature-level sparsity identification
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: Parameter elimination (Venzon & Moolgavkar 1988) and adaptive ridge regression equivalence (Grandvalet 1998) are established techniques; contribution is primarily their application to this architecture

Strong model assumptions underexplored: The core assumption that data decomposes as 'linear + nonlinear corrections' is restrictive and may not hold for highly nonlinear data; insufficient investigation of when this fails, acknowledged only briefly in conclusions

Interpretability claims need stronger empirical support: While β_j has clear interpretation, per-instance explanations still come from a black-box NN; no visualization of learned g_u_j functions; no direct quantitative comparison of explanation quality vs. SHAP or other post-hoc methods beyond feature ranking

Real-world empirical results underwhelming: Only 3 real datasets tested; predictive performance on real data (Figure 5) often comparable or inferior to vanilla NN and other baselines; large overlapping error bars without significance tests; superconductivity results (81 features) show unclear sparsity patterns

Insufficient comparison with similar methods: IMN (predicting per-instance linear coefficients) is conceptually very similar but key differences underdeveloped; deeper analysis of when NIMO outperforms IMN and LassoNet needed

Ad-hoc implementation choices lacking principled justification: Sin activation function (unusual, not well-motivated), group L2 only on first layer, noise injection for sparsity enforcement (heuristic, not theoretically grounded), binary positional encoding choice; interplay between penalties not theoretically analyzed

Missing critical analyses: No investigation of what nonlinearities g_u_j actually learns; Boston dataset feature 'B' anomaly (Figure 12) unexplained; limited analysis of when/why method works vs. fails; synthetic data success expected since data matches model form

Scalability concerns not addressed: No computational complexity analysis; largest real dataset (81 features) modest; unclear how positional encoding scales to very high dimensions common in modern applications

strengths: Well-motivated hybrid approach addressing genuine tension between interpretability and expressivity
Elegant architectural design with masking mechanism (g_uj(x_-j)) ensuring linear interpretability of coefficients
Mathematically sound parameter elimination optimization technique extending to Lasso via adaptive ridge regression
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with ground-truth validation on synthetic data, showing correct coefficient recovery and sparsity learning
Thorough ablation studies validating design choices (masking, position encoding) and extension to classification
Honest discussion of fundamental limitations (self-interactions) with proposed remedies (basis expansion)
Local explanations aligned with SHAP values (Figure 19) demonstrating consistency with post-hoc methods
Extensive implementation details and additional experiments in appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Fundamental expressivity limitation: Cannot learn self-interactions (x_j^2, etc.) due to architectural constraint, severely limiting applicability (Table 4 shows 5.34 MSE vs 1.027 for LassoNet)
Interpretability claims lack empirical validation: No user studies to show MEM is actually more interpretable to practitioners; Table 2 shows method disagreement on real data with no ground truth
Limited novelty over existing work: Core idea of linear base + learned corrections exists in NAM/LassoNet/IMN; distinction of preserving global linearity through masking is incremental

MEM limitations underexplored: Paper acknowledges MEM can fail for highly nonlinear functions but argues NIMO's explicit linear component justifies it—circular reasoning that sidesteps the core trade-off
Weak experimental validation on real data: Only 3 datasets; PMLB benchmarks (D.10) show underperformance on some tasks; no formal accuracy-interpretability trade-off metrics
Technical gaps: Invertibility conditions for Eq. (5) not guaranteed; IRLS convergence properties for GLMs not analyzed; no generalization theory
Synthetic experiments favor NIMO: Ground truth is constructed as linear + nonlinear corrections, naturally biasing toward methods preserving linearity
Hyperparameter sensitivity not addressed: Multiple penalties (λ, μ, λ_group) tuned via grid search without sensitivity analysis or principled selection methods

strengths: Clear problem motivation and well-articulated tension between interpretability and expressivity
Technically sound parameter elimination optimization with extensions to GLMs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including synthetic data, real datasets, and ablation studies
Honest acknowledgment of architectural limitations (cannot capture self-interactions)
Generally well-written with intuitive figures and detailed appendices
weaknesses: Limited novelty: multiplicative corrections and parameter elimination build on known techniques (profile likelihood, adaptive ridge regression)
Severe architectural constraint (excluding x_j from g_u_j) not well justified; prevents capturing important self-interactions; workaround requires manual feature engineering

MEM interpretability claims problematic: (1) circular reasoning—model designed to make MEM=β by construction, (2) inadequate handling of MEM's acknowledged general limitations, (3) standardization requirement limits applicability, (4) empirical evidence mixed (Table 2 shows disagreement across methods)
Mixed empirical results on real datasets: NIMO comparable to simpler baselines (Lasso on diabetes), no clear advantage over vanilla NNs on Boston housing and superconductivity

Incomplete evaluation of actual interpretability: no user studies, no comparison with interpretability baselines, local explanation validation circular (SHAP comparison), ground truth recovery only on synthetic data
Unclear practical guidance: when should practitioners use NIMO vs. alternatives? Missing computational cost analysis and scalability discussion
Experimental design favors method: synthetic datasets designed to match NIMO's multiplicative architecture; real dataset disagreements (Figure 5, Table 2) undermine interpretability claims
Gap between claims and evidence: paper claims to combine 'best of both worlds' but severely restricted expressivity and no demonstrated interpretability advantages in realistic settings

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff with clear conceptual distinction between global (MEM) and local explanations
Solid technical framework with clever architectural design (guj(0)=0, x-j masking) ensuring linear coefficient interpretability while enabling nonlinear corrections
Novel application of parameter elimination for joint optimization of linear coefficients and NN parameters, with principled extension to adaptive ridge regression
Comprehensive and well-designed experimental evaluation including synthetic data with ground truth, multiple strong baselines, extensive ablations, and reproducibility details
Generally clear presentation with informative figures, well-organized structure, and thorough supplementary materials
weaknesses: Significant architectural limitation: inability to capture self-interactions (x²j, etc.) due to constraint that guj depends only on x-j; workaround requires feature engineering, undermining interpretability benefits

Weak real-world evaluation: on 3 datasets tested, NIMO achieves only comparable (not superior) performance to baselines; diabetes shows no clear advantage, Boston/superconductivity match standard methods, providing limited evidence of practical value

Marginal Effects at Mean (MEM) limitations inadequately addressed: Table 2 shows MEM diverges from SHAP rankings on Boston housing; explanation via 'feature selection instability' raises questions about whether MEM captures meaningful stable interpretations

Interpretability evaluation not rigorous: paper focuses heavily on predictive performance; lacks systematic comparison of interpretability quality across methods and does not validate that NIMO's interpretations are more meaningful/stable than alternatives

Limited novelty: combines existing techniques (hybrid models, parameter elimination via profile likelihood, adaptive ridge regression); main contribution is specific architectural choice, which is somewhat incremental

Missing theoretical and empirical guidance: no characterization of when NIMO outperforms alternatives, no analysis of approximation quality, no convergence guarantees, and no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameter choices
Implementation-theory gap: theoretical model uses d separate networks but implementation uses single shared network with positional encoding plus noise injection (workaround for sparsity enforcement)

Experimental concerns: no statistical significance testing in Table 1; inconsistent baseline performance (e.g., NAM underperforms Lasso on synthetic additive data despite designed for this setting) deserves explanation
